screens.title: What an Upgrade Does — proxy vs implementation
screens.narratorSegment: An upgrade replaces the implementation contract while the proxy remains the same. That is the core claim: the proxy address and its storage persist, and only the target logic address changes. Practically, when a proxy delegates a call after an upgrade it invokes new code but reads the same storage slots it always did. A concrete example: you deployed UpgradeableNFT (V1) with a token counter stored at a specific slot. After upgrading to UpgradeableNFT_V2, the token counter lives in the same slot, so token IDs continue from the same next value. A common misconception is to assume that deploying a new implementation moves data into the new contract. It doesn't; storage stays with the proxy, so any mismatch in variable order or type between V1 and V2 can make the proxy read the wrong slot and corrupt data. One useful mental model is to think of the proxy as a fixed filing cabinet of data and the implementation as a set of rules that read from the cabinet; if the rules expect items in different drawers, the results will be wrong. Takeaway: upgrades change logic, not storage — always preserve layout compatibility before proceeding.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › What an Upgrade Does
Core Concept

Proxy vs Implementation

The proxy holds storage and delegates calls; the implementation contains logic and is replaced during an upgrade.
Example
Your token counter in V1 remains valid in V2 because the proxy still stores the counter at the same slot.
Misconception
Deploying V2 does not copy state into V2. If variable order changes, the proxy will read the wrong slots.
Key Takeaway

Treat the proxy as the single source of truth for state; preserve the mapping from variable names to storage slots across upgrades.

Analogy
Think of the proxy as a locked toolbox with numbered drawers. Implementations are instruction sheets that say which drawer to read. If a new sheet expects different drawer numbers, you will open the wrong drawer.
Check your understanding: If a new implementation adds a variable at the end, will existing storage read correctly? Why or why not?

screens.title: Upgrade Workflow with Hardhat
screens.narratorSegment: When using Hardhat with OpenZeppelin upgrades, the upgrade process follows a simple, safe workflow. First, prepare your new implementation contract source and ensure storage layout compatibility. Next, run prepareUpgrade with the proxy address and the new contract factory; this deploys an implementation candidate and runs the plugin's storage layout checks. PrepareUpgrade returns the new implementation address so you can inspect it before switching the proxy. Finally, call upgrades. upgradeProxy with the proxy address and your new contract factory. This deploys and wires the proxy to the new implementation in one coordinated sequence. A concrete example is the provided script that prints the new implementation address, performs upgradeProxy, waits for deployment, and then calls V2-only functions. A common pitfall is to skip prepareUpgrade; that avoids automated layout checks and risks data corruption. Also remember gas: deploying a new implementation and sending an upgrade transaction cost gas; rehearsal on a testnet will surface surprises. As a quick checklist: verify code compiles, run prepareUpgrade, run your tests against V2 code using the proxy, and then execute upgradeProxy through a controlled signer. Afterward, confirm by calling a V2-only getter through the proxy.

screens.title: UpgradeableNFT_V2 — Solidity changes
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the UpgradeableNFT_V2 contract. The essential idea is minimal, deliberate change: V2 reuses the same inherited upgradeable base and adds exactly one new state variable at the end, plus a setter function. The constructor disables initializers, and initialize sets up inherited modules and the token counter. Critically, newFeatureMessage appears after _tokenIdCounter so existing storage slot assignments remain intact. Concretely, safeMint and getNextTokenId continue to operate against the same counter stored in the proxy. A concrete misuse is inserting newFeatureMessage before existing variables; the storage layout check will fail because variable order changed, or worse, if the check were bypassed, it would shift slots and corrupt state. When using this V2, either add a new initializer that migrates or use a setter to set initial values; do not call the original initialize on an already-initialized proxy. Misconception to avoid: changing function signatures or adding new functions is fine; storage layout is the only part that demands strict ordering. Takeaway: add variables at the end, keep the rest unchanged, and use setters or a migration initializer for new state values.

keyIdea.text: Add new state only at the end; function changes are allowed, storage changes are not.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › UpgradeableNFT_V2
Solidity — V2 highlights
// contracts/UpgradeableNFT_V2.sol
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.20;

import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/token/ERC721/ERC721Upgradeable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/access/OwnableUpgradeable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/proxy/utils/Initializable.sol";
import "@openzeppelin/contracts-upgradeable/utils/CountersUpgradeable.sol";

contract UpgradeableNFT_V2 is Initializable, ERC721Upgradeable, OwnableUpgradeable {
  using CountersUpgradeable for CountersUpgradeable.Counter;
  CountersUpgradeable.Counter private _tokenIdCounter;

  // NEW: Add a new state variable. It MUST be added at the end.
  string public newFeatureMessage;

  /// @custom:oz-upgrades-unsafe-allow constructor
  constructor() {
    _disableInitializers();
  }

  function initialize(string memory name, string memory symbol) initializer public {
    __ERC721_init(name, symbol);
    __Ownable_init(msg.sender);
    _tokenIdCounter.increment(); // Start from 1
  }

  function safeMint(address to) public onlyOwner {
    uint252 tokenId = _tokenIdCounter.current();
    _tokenIdCounter.increment();
    _safeMint(to, tokenId);
  }

  function getNextTokenId() public view returns (uint256) {
    return _tokenIdCounter.current();
  }

  function setNewFeatureMessage(string memory _message) public onlyOwner {
    newFeatureMessage = _message;
  }
}
Note: newFeatureMessage is intentionally not initialized in initialize; a setter or migration initializer can set it after upgrade.
Why placement matters
Adding newFeatureMessage at the end preserves the previously assigned storage slots for _tokenIdCounter and inherited variables.
Misconception
Functions may change freely; however, storage layout is the immutable mapping that must remain compatible.
Key Takeaway

Small, intentional storage additions at the end are safe. Never reorder or change types of existing variables.

screens.title: Hardhat Upgrade Script Explained
screens.narratorSegment: The Hardhat script does three notable actions. It first retrieves a contract factory for the V2 implementation. Next, it calls prepareUpgrade with the proxy address and the V2 factory. PrepareUpgrade is important because it deploys the candidate implementation and runs the OpenZeppelin plugin’s storage layout checks — it will fail if compatibility rules are violated. This gives you a chance to inspect the implementation address and abort if something looks wrong. Finally, the script calls upgrades. upgradeProxy, which coordinates deploying and pointing the proxy at the new logic. The example script then waits for the upgraded contract to be deployed, reads a V2-only getter, and calls a setter to verify the new behavior. A common trap is using an account that lacks upgrade authority; always execute upgrades from a controlled signer such as a multisig key or a timelocked admin. Also run tests that exercise existing storage reads via the proxy after upgrade to ensure behavior is preserved. Takeaway: prepareUpgrade is your safety gate and upgradeProxy performs the final wiring; use both in sequence and verify results in your test environment before any Mainnet action.

// scripts/upgradeUpgradeableNFT.js (excerpt)
const { ethers, upgrades } = require("hardhat");

const UpgradeableNFT_V2 = await ethers.getContractFactory("UpgradeableNFT_V2");

// Safety check + deploy implementation candidate

// script/UpgradeUpgradeableNFT.s.sol (excerpt)
contract UpgradeUpgradeableNFT is Script {
  function run() public {
    vm.startBroadcast();

    address proxyAddress = 0x...; // Replace with your deployed proxy address

    UpgradeableNFT_V2 newImplementation = new UpgradeableNFT_V2();

    // Upgrade the proxy to point to the new implementation
    Proxy.upgrade(proxyAddress, address(newImplementation));

    vm.stopBroadcast();
  }
}

Foundry scripts let you express upgrades in Solidity and broadcast from the CLI, ideal for repeatable automation.
Misconception
The checks are not optional: OpenZeppelin's foundry upgrades perform storage layout validation, just like Hardhat.

screens.title: Storage Layout Compatibility
screens.narratorSegment: Storage layout compatibility is the most critical rule when upgrading proxy-based contracts. The rule set is concise: do not change the order of existing state variables, do not change their types, and only add new state variables at the end of the storage layout. Why these constraints? Solidity assigns storage slots sequentially; if you shift the order, the variables previously stored by the proxy will be interpreted differently by the new implementation, causing corrupted reads and potentially catastrophic behavior. A concrete example from the chapter: adding a boolean at the beginning of TokenLock_V2 will shift all subsequent variables and trigger a prepareUpgrade failure. The OpenZeppelin plugins automatically detect such incompatibilities and refuse the upgrade, which is why you should never bypass these checks. A common misconception is that you can always migrate by copying values from the old implementation; in proxy patterns, storage is not moved to the new implementation. Instead, plan new variables at the end, and if you need to transform stored data, do it via a migration function or a carefully-designed initializer that runs only once. Takeaway: treat storage layout rules as immutable constraints for safe upgrades.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Storage Layout Compatibility

Storage Layout Compatibility

Rules and rationale
Rules
  • Do not change the order of existing state variables.
  • Do not change the type of existing state variables.
  • New variables may be added only at the end of the layout.
Why it matters
Solidity assigns storage sequentially. Changing order changes the mapping of variable names to storage slots, causing the proxy to read incorrect values after an upgrade.
Example
TokenLock_V1 had owner and lockAmount. Adding isPaused at the beginning in V2 shifts all slots and will fail prepareUpgrade or corrupt state if unchecked.

screens.title: Common Pitfalls & Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: Upgrades introduce several practical risks you must spot and mitigate. First, storage collisions: inserting or changing variables will shift storage slots and corrupt data. The OpenZeppelin plugin helps catch this, but never skip those checks. Second, re-initializing: calling initialize on an already-initialized proxy can break invariants. The initializer modifier prevents accidental re-initialization, but a malicious or mistaken call to initialize in V2 could be dangerous if you wrote a migration initializer incorrectly. Third, access control: ensure only a multisig or DAO-controlled key can perform upgrades. If a single private key can upgrade logic, a compromise could replace your implementation with malicious code. Fourth, operational costs: deploying a new implementation and sending an upgrade transaction consume gas; plan budgets for Mainnet. A useful comparison is: code changes are flexible, storage changes are rigid. Example contrast: adding new functions is safe and encouraged; adding or reordering storage variables is not. Takeaway: always run automated plugin checks, rehearse on testnets, and gate upgrades behind secure operational controls. Common Pitfalls & Misconceptions means watch for storage collisions, avoid re-initialization, enforce strict upgrade authority, and plan for gas costs.. In practical terms, storage collisions, re-initialization, and authority risks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: Upgrades introduce several practical risks you must spot and mitigate. First, storage collisions: inserting or changing variables will shift storage slots and corrupt data. The OpenZeppelin plugin helps catch this, but never skip those checks. Second, re-initializing: calling initialize on an already-initialized proxy can break invariants. The initializer modifier prevents accidental re-initialization, but a malicious or mistaken call to initialize in V2 could be dangerous if you wrote a migration initializer incorrectly. Third, access control: ensure only a multisig or DAO-controlled key can perform upgrades. If a single private key can upgrade logic, a compromise could replace your implementation with malicious code. Fourth, operational costs: deploying a new implementation and sending an upgrade transaction consume gas; plan budgets for Mainnet. A useful comparison is: code changes are flexible, storage changes are rigid. Example contrast: adding new functions is safe and encouraged; adding or reordering storage variables is not. Takeaway: always run automated plugin checks, rehearse on testnets, and gate upgrades behind secure operational controls. Module 7 › Chapter 7.6 › Common Pitfalls
Storage collisions
Inserting variables in the middle or changing types will shift storage slots. The plugin will typically block such upgrades.
Re-initialization
Do not call initialize on a proxy that already ran initialization. Use migration initializers carefully.
Access control
Restrict upgrades to a multisig or timelocked admin to reduce risk from compromised keys.
Gas & operations
Upgrades cost gas for deployment and the upgrade transaction. Rehearse on testnets to estimate costs.
Plugin reliance
Rely on OpenZeppelin plugin checks rather than ad-hoc manual verification; they catch many subtle issues.
Key Takeaway

Treat upgrades as maintenance windows: test, gate, and verify each step to avoid irreversible state corruption.

screens.title: Operational Safety: Timelocks and Emergency Pause
screens.narratorSegment: In production systems, upgrades should never be instantaneous and unrestricted. Two operational controls are emphasized: timelocks and emergency pause mechanisms. A timelock introduces a delay between proposing and executing an upgrade. This delay gives the community and auditors time to review the proposed implementation, and it allows cancellation if a malicious change is detected. Emergency pause adds a short-circuit that can halt critical operations, buying time to initiate an upgrade or mitigation plan. For example, if a token transfer function misbehaves after an upgrade, a pause can prevent further losses while you coordinate an emergency patch. Testing practices complement these controls: run unit and integration tests against the V2 implementation through the proxy on testnets, and consider fuzz testing to probe edge cases. A common misconception is that these controls replace careful code review; they do not. They are mitigations that buy time and transparency but should be used alongside rigorous testing and access control. Takeaway: pair technical checks with operational gates — automated layout checks, timelocks for public upgrades, and emergency pause for rapid mitigation. screens.title: Checklist: Before You Upgrade
screens.narratorSegment: Before executing any upgrade on a production system, run a checklist that combines automated checks and operational approvals. Start with automated static checks and compilation. Next, run the OpenZeppelin plugin’s prepareUpgrade to perform storage layout validation and capture the candidate implementation address. Run your full test suite against the V2 code, and then run integration tests against the existing proxy on a testnet to ensure reads and writes still behave as expected. Obtain operational approvals: signers from a multisig or a governance proposal and, if appropriate, a timelock scheduling the upgrade transaction. Ensure you have an emergency pause plan and an identifiable rollback or migration plan in case something goes wrong. Record gas estimates from testnet runs and ensure the deployer has sufficient funds. After the upgrade, verify the implementation address and call a V2-only function through the proxy to confirm success. A common misconception is that a passing unit test is sufficient; it is not — test the whole system with the proxy in place. Takeaway: follow an automated checklist plus human approval to reduce risk. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll learn the practical steps to upgrade a deployed, proxy-backed contract without losing state. You will understand that an upgrade replaces only the logic contract while the proxy’s address and stored data remain unchanged. I’ll show you why storage layout compatibility is the single most important rule, and how tools like OpenZeppelin’s Hardhat and Foundry plugins check layout before permitting an upgrade. We will also walk through a concrete V2 example that adds a new state variable at the end, a Hardhat upgrade script that uses prepareUpgrade and upgradeProxy, and a Foundry script variant that performs the same actions. Finally, we’ll cover the operational safeguards you must apply: access control for who can trigger upgrades, testnet rehearsal, timelocks for production, and emergency pause patterns. By the end you’ll be able to prepare an implementation, run plugin checks, execute an upgrade on a testnet, and verify the new implementation address. Consider one question as you begin: what state would break if a new variable were inserted at the start of your contract?

By the end of this chapter you will prepare and execute safe upgrades for proxy-based contracts. First, you will learn how to write a new implementation that is storage-layout compatible with an existing proxy and how to deploy it so the proxy can point to the new logic. Second, you will be able to use OpenZeppelin’s Hardhat and Foundry plugins to run pre-upgrade storage checks and carry out the upgrade transaction. Third, you will gain a checklist of safety practices: controlled access to upgrade keys, testnet rehearsal, timelocks for production, and emergency pause mechanisms for rapid mitigation. Finally, you will learn how to verify that the proxy now points to the new implementation and exercise added functions safely. Each objective includes a concrete example or mnemonic to help you retain the rule, and a verified competency milestone so you know when you’ve practiced the skill correctly.

This second objectives slide focuses on concrete verification steps and the mental model you should carry forward. You will be able to run prepareUpgrade to get an implementation address and to interpret its warnings. You should also know how to run upgradeProxy and confirm that the proxy now resolves to the new implementation address. In Foundry, you will deploy a new implementation and call Proxy. upgrade to change the pointer. For verification, you will inspect the proxy on a block explorer to confirm the implementation address changed and call a V2-only function to demonstrate the upgrade succeeded. A common misconception is that upgrading moves stored state into the new contract; remind yourself that the proxy keeps all storage and the implementation contains only logic. Your competency milestone is a successful testnet upgrade followed by a read of a newly added state value using the proxy interface.

An upgrade replaces the implementation contract while the proxy remains the same. That is the core claim: the proxy address and its storage persist, and only the target logic address changes. Practically, when a proxy delegates a call after an upgrade it invokes new code but reads the same storage slots it always did. A concrete example: you deployed UpgradeableNFT (V1) with a token counter stored at a specific slot. After upgrading to UpgradeableNFT_V2, the token counter lives in the same slot, so token IDs continue from the same next value. A common misconception is to assume that deploying a new implementation moves data into the new contract. It doesn't; storage stays with the proxy, so any mismatch in variable order or type between V1 and V2 can make the proxy read the wrong slot and corrupt data. One useful mental model is to think of the proxy as a fixed filing cabinet of data and the implementation as a set of rules that read from the cabinet; if the rules expect items in different drawers, the results will be wrong. Takeaway: upgrades change logic, not storage — always preserve layout compatibility before proceeding.

When using Hardhat with OpenZeppelin upgrades, the upgrade process follows a simple, safe workflow. First, prepare your new implementation contract source and ensure storage layout compatibility. Next, run prepareUpgrade with the proxy address and the new contract factory; this deploys an implementation candidate and runs the plugin's storage layout checks. PrepareUpgrade returns the new implementation address so you can inspect it before switching the proxy. Finally, call upgrades. upgradeProxy with the proxy address and your new contract factory. This deploys and wires the proxy to the new implementation in one coordinated sequence. A concrete example is the provided script that prints the new implementation address, performs upgradeProxy, waits for deployment, and then calls V2-only functions. A common pitfall is to skip prepareUpgrade; that avoids automated layout checks and risks data corruption. Also remember gas: deploying a new implementation and sending an upgrade transaction cost gas; rehearsal on a testnet will surface surprises. As a quick checklist: verify code compiles, run prepareUpgrade, run your tests against V2 code using the proxy, and then execute upgradeProxy through a controlled signer. Afterward, confirm by calling a V2-only getter through the proxy.

Let's walk through the UpgradeableNFT_V2 contract. The essential idea is minimal, deliberate change: V2 reuses the same inherited upgradeable base and adds exactly one new state variable at the end, plus a setter function. The constructor disables initializers, and initialize sets up inherited modules and the token counter. Critically, newFeatureMessage appears after _tokenIdCounter so existing storage slot assignments remain intact. Concretely, safeMint and getNextTokenId continue to operate against the same counter stored in the proxy. A concrete misuse is inserting newFeatureMessage before existing variables; the storage layout check will fail because variable order changed, or worse, if the check were bypassed, it would shift slots and corrupt state. When using this V2, either add a new initializer that migrates or use a setter to set initial values; do not call the original initialize on an already-initialized proxy. Misconception to avoid: changing function signatures or adding new functions is fine; storage layout is the only part that demands strict ordering. Takeaway: add variables at the end, keep the rest unchanged, and use setters or a migration initializer for new state values.

The Hardhat script does three notable actions. It first retrieves a contract factory for the V2 implementation. Next, it calls prepareUpgrade with the proxy address and the V2 factory. PrepareUpgrade is important because it deploys the candidate implementation and runs the OpenZeppelin plugin’s storage layout checks — it will fail if compatibility rules are violated. This gives you a chance to inspect the implementation address and abort if something looks wrong. Finally, the script calls upgrades. upgradeProxy, which coordinates deploying and pointing the proxy at the new logic. The example script then waits for the upgraded contract to be deployed, reads a V2-only getter, and calls a setter to verify the new behavior. A common trap is using an account that lacks upgrade authority; always execute upgrades from a controlled signer such as a multisig key or a timelocked admin. Also run tests that exercise existing storage reads via the proxy after upgrade to ensure behavior is preserved. Takeaway: prepareUpgrade is your safety gate and upgradeProxy performs the final wiring; use both in sequence and verify results in your test environment before any Mainnet action.

Foundry supports upgradeable workflows via the OpenZeppelin forge-upgrades tooling. The typical flow is similar to Hardhat: compile and deploy the new implementation, then call a library function that updates the proxy pointer. In the example Script contract, you deploy UpgradeableNFT_V2, then call Proxy. upgrade with the proxy address and the new implementation address. This action performs storage layout checks just like the Hardhat plugin. An important practical point is to use the same safety mindset: broadcast the script with a controlled key and run it on Sepolia first. Foundry’s script runs inside a broadcast session so it can both deploy and send the upgrade transaction. A frequent misconception is that Foundry’s tooling is less strict than OpenZeppelin’s Hardhat plugin; in fact, the OpenZeppelin-foundry-upgrades checks storage compatibility as well. After the upgrade, log and inspect the new implementation address, then call a V2-only function via the proxy to validate the change. Finally, remember to pass appropriate RPC and gas settings so the broadcast completes successfully. Takeaway: Foundry offers the same guarded upgrade path but in a solidity-script style suitable for developer automation.

Storage layout compatibility is the most critical rule when upgrading proxy-based contracts. The rule set is concise: do not change the order of existing state variables, do not change their types, and only add new state variables at the end of the storage layout. Why these constraints? Solidity assigns storage slots sequentially; if you shift the order, the variables previously stored by the proxy will be interpreted differently by the new implementation, causing corrupted reads and potentially catastrophic behavior. A concrete example from the chapter: adding a boolean at the beginning of TokenLock_V2 will shift all subsequent variables and trigger a prepareUpgrade failure. The OpenZeppelin plugins automatically detect such incompatibilities and refuse the upgrade, which is why you should never bypass these checks. A common misconception is that you can always migrate by copying values from the old implementation; in proxy patterns, storage is not moved to the new implementation. Instead, plan new variables at the end, and if you need to transform stored data, do it via a migration function or a carefully-designed initializer that runs only once. Takeaway: treat storage layout rules as immutable constraints for safe upgrades.

Upgrades introduce several practical risks you must spot and mitigate. First, storage collisions: inserting or changing variables will shift storage slots and corrupt data. The OpenZeppelin plugin helps catch this, but never skip those checks. Second, re-initializing: calling initialize on an already-initialized proxy can break invariants. The initializer modifier prevents accidental re-initialization, but a malicious or mistaken call to initialize in V2 could be dangerous if you wrote a migration initializer incorrectly. Third, access control: ensure only a multisig or DAO-controlled key can perform upgrades. If a single private key can upgrade logic, a compromise could replace your implementation with malicious code. Fourth, operational costs: deploying a new implementation and sending an upgrade transaction consume gas; plan budgets for Mainnet. A useful comparison is: code changes are flexible, storage changes are rigid. Example contrast: adding new functions is safe and encouraged; adding or reordering storage variables is not. Takeaway: always run automated plugin checks, rehearse on testnets, and gate upgrades behind secure operational controls. In production systems, upgrades should never be instantaneous and unrestricted. Two operational controls are emphasized: timelocks and emergency pause mechanisms. A timelock introduces a delay between proposing and executing an upgrade. This delay gives the community and auditors time to review the proposed implementation, and it allows cancellation if a malicious change is detected. Emergency pause adds a short-circuit that can halt critical operations, buying time to initiate an upgrade or mitigation plan. For example, if a token transfer function misbehaves after an upgrade, a pause can prevent further losses while you coordinate an emergency patch. Testing practices complement these controls: run unit and integration tests against the V2 implementation through the proxy on testnets, and consider fuzz testing to probe edge cases. A common misconception is that these controls replace careful code review; they do not. They are mitigations that buy time and transparency but should be used alongside rigorous testing and access control. Takeaway: pair technical checks with operational gates — automated layout checks, timelocks for public upgrades, and emergency pause for rapid mitigation. Before executing any upgrade on a production system, run a checklist that combines automated checks and operational approvals. Start with automated static checks and compilation. Next, run the OpenZeppelin plugin’s prepareUpgrade to perform storage layout validation and capture the candidate implementation address. Run your full test suite against the V2 code, and then run integration tests against the existing proxy on a testnet to ensure reads and writes still behave as expected. Obtain operational approvals: signers from a multisig or a governance proposal and, if appropriate, a timelock scheduling the upgrade transaction. Ensure you have an emergency pause plan and an identifiable rollback or migration plan in case something goes wrong. Record gas estimates from testnet runs and ensure the deployer has sufficient funds. After the upgrade, verify the implementation address and call a V2-only function through the proxy to confirm success. A common misconception is that a passing unit test is sufficient; it is not — test the whole system with the proxy in place. Takeaway: follow an automated checklist plus human approval to reduce risk. Here are the compact concepts to carry forward. First, upgrade transactions change only the implementation pointer; the proxy address and storage remain intact. Second, storage layout compatibility is mandatory: never change the order or types of existing state variables, and add new variables only at the end. Third, use the OpenZeppelin upgrade plugins to run prepareUpgrade and avoid manual mistakes; they automate storage checks and prevent dangerous upgrades. Keep these three concepts at the top of your checklist when planning any upgrade, and pair them with operational controls like multisigs, timelocks, and emergency pause for production safety.
